title: The Mishnah
hook: six orders of oral teaching, written down so they wouldn't be lost

segments.voice: Yesterday, nasi: Judah the Prince gave the oral teaching a shape. Your line was writing it down. Today, we open what he made.

The book begins with a question, and not a grand one. From when may a person recite the Shema in the evening? No creation story. No hero. Just a practical question about a prayer said every night, and right away three answers: Rabbi Eliezer says one thing, the sages another, Rabban Gamaliel a third. Then a little story. Gamaliel's sons come home late from a wedding feast and tell their father they haven't said the Shema yet. The night is far along. Is it too late? That is how the Mishnah opens: a family, a late night, and a room full of teachers who don't all agree.
screen: `FROM WHEN, IN THE EVENING?` → `THREE ANSWERS.` → `SONS HOME LATE FROM A WEDDING.`

segments.voice: The Mishnah is teaching that tradition calls oral Torah: the explanation that, in Jewish belief, traveled alongside the written Torah, taught teacher to student and learned by heart. Tradition ties the name to a Hebrew word for repeating, because it was learned by saying it over and over. Now it is written. Six orders, each called a seder. The Talmud later finds all six in a single verse of Isaiah, one word for each: seeds and farming, appointed times and festivals, women and marriage, damages, holy things, and purities. Inside the orders are tractates, inside the tractates chapters, and inside each chapter short units, each also called a mishnah. So the word names the whole book and one small piece of it. What surprises a first reader is that the Mishnah keeps the minority opinion. Back to that first page. The sages say the evening Shema may be said until midnight. Rabban Gamaliel says until dawn. So when his sons come home late, he tells them: if the dawn hasn't come up, you are still obliged to say it. And the page records both views, with names attached. Disagreement isn't erased when the teaching is written down. It's kept, carefully, as part of the teaching. The oral, written, still sounds like people talking.
screen: `ORAL TORAH, NOW ON THE PAGE.` · `SIX ORDERS, FOUND IN ONE VERSE.` · then, large: `THE MINORITY VIEW IS KEPT.` · `GAMALIEL: UNTIL DAWN.`

segments.voice: Here is the first mishnah in plain words. From when may the Shema be said in the evening? From the hour the priests go in to eat their holy portion; until when? Rabbi Eliezer says until the end of the first watch of the night, the sages say until midnight, and Rabban Gamaliel says until dawn. Hold the three answers side by side, nobody erased, and if you pray, say a short evening prayer you know; if not, rest with the question: what in your life is still not too late?
Mishnah. The oral teaching, written down and arranged in six orders. The word names the whole book, and also each short unit inside it.
Your line: the oral, written. Three answers on one page, and every one kept. Day nine hundred seven, done.

howItsDone: Jews study Mishnah in small portions, and some learn a chapter in memory of someone who has died; it is studied in yeshivas, synagogues and at home, often aloud with a partner.
